question.knowledge_point: Determining the Behavior of a Function in the Neighborhood of a Point
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13831128/assets/fa15192923f9fd7370818fcb6b05b24b3bb6901dfbf90dd53539d71fd0f8b0bf.png)

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following statements are true? 

I. $f(x)$ is defined at $x=2$

II. ${lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x)=f(2)$

III. $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=2$
question.worked_solution:
By inspecting the graph, we can conclude the following:

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $f(x)$ is defined at $x=2$ and $f(2)=1.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, from the graph we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{-}}f(x) & =1, \\ {lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}f(x) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x)=1=f(2).$

- Statement III is true. The graph of $f(x)$ can be drawn without taking our pencil off of the paper in the neighborhood of $x=2.$

judgment.reasoning: All three earlier selections agree with the supplied graphs and their own captured solutions. For q-78132, the graph is continuous at -2 and 3, but has unequal one-sided limits at 1, so I and III only are true. For q-48062, the hole at (1,1) leaves f(1) undefined while both one-sided limits equal 1; only II is true. For q-48065, f(2)=1 and both one-sided limits equal 1, so all three statements are true. The corner at x=2 does not prevent continuity.
